overview.body:
**Iásōn** ​(*iason*) — ‌Captain of ‌the Argo ​· Seeker ​of the ​Golden Fleece ​— ​belongs to ‌the Greek ​tradition, where ​it is ‌catalogued under ​the domain ‌"Heroism, the ​Golden ‌Fleece". The ​name means ​"Healer"[^1].

Iásōn ​is the ​captain of ​the first ‌great ​sea-quest of ‌Greek myth: ​the voyage ‌of the ​Argo to ‌Colchis for ​the ‌Golden Fleece. ​His name ​comes from ‌**ἰάομαι, 'to ‌heal'** — ‌yet his ​story is ​less ‌about curing ​than about ​gathering: he ‌is the ​hero whose ​greatest power ‌is ​to summon ‌other heroes, ​and to ​win the ​love of ​a princess ‌whose ‌magic does ​the work.[^2]

‌PuniCodex restores ​the name ​as **Iásōn** ‌and serves ‌its temple ‌at ‌[iásōn.com](https://xn--isn-ela55c.com). The ​original carries ‌both stress ​and vowel ​length, and ​exactly one ‌historically ​valid Unicode ​restoration exists, ​which places ‌the name ​in Tier ​1. The ​plain ‌ASCII form ​*iason* survives ‌as a ​modern convenience ‌imposed by ​the early ‌domain-name system; ‌the ​restoration, not ​the fallback, ​is the ​form the ‌project defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

the-name.body:
The ​name is ‌attested ‌in Greek ​as ​**Ἰάσων**. Etymologically ​it ​means "Healer"[^1].

​The ‌ASCII form ​*iason* ​survives only ‌because the ​early ‌domain-name system ​could ‌not carry ​diacritics; ​it is ​a ​technological compromise, ​not ‌an ancient ​spelling. ‌The Unicode ​restoration ‌**Iásōn** recovers ​both ‌the stress ​accent ‌and the ​vowel ​length of ‌the original ‌directly ‌in the ​address ​bar. The ‌original ​carries both ​stress ‌and vowel ​length, ​and exactly ‌one ​historically valid ‌Unicode ​restoration exists, ​which ​places the ​name ‌in Tier ‌1.

​The letter-by-letter ‌transformation ​runs:

- ​**i** → ‌**I** ‌— I ‌uppercase
‌- **a** ​→ ‌**á** — ​Acute ​on a
​- ‌**s** → ​**s** ​— s ​same
‌- **o** ​→ ​**ō** — ​Macron: ‌long vowel
​- ‌**n** → ​**n** — ‌n ​same

The ‌project ‌holds the ​domain ​**iásōn.com** (xn--isn-ela55c.com) ​as ​the canonical ‌home ‌of this ​name[^2].

sources.citation: Liddell-Scott-Jones Greek-English Lexicon, 9th ed. with 1996 supplement, 1940.
Etymological Dictionary of Greek, 2 vols., Brill, 2010.

pronunciation.body:
The reconstructed ​pronunciation of ‌the name is ‌**/i.áː.sɔːn/** — ​Attic Greek Reconstruction.[^1]

​Phoneme by ​phoneme:

- ​**I-** — Short ​iota with ‌smooth breathing — ​the name ​opens light and ‌quick, without ​roughness.
- **-á-** ‌— Long ​alpha with acute ‌pitch [áː] ​— the ​stressed peak of ​the name; ​the Ionic form ​Ἰήσων, with ‌long eta, proves ​the vowel's ‌length.
- **-sōn** ​— Sigma ‌followed by long ​omega [sɔːn] ‌— the ​drawn-out final syllable ‌that marks ​the name as ​long-voweled.

For ‌the modern speaker, ‌the closest ‌approximation is: 'ih-AH-sone' ​— the ​second syllable is ‌pitched higher ​and held; ​the final 'ō' ‌is long ​and closed, nothing ​like the ‌English 'sun'.

Kindred ​and historical ‌forms of the ​name:

- ​**Greek verb** — ​ἰάομαι, 'to ​heal, to ‌cure' — the ‌root of ​the name
- ‌**Greek noun** ​— ἰατρός, 'physician', ​built on ‌the same root
‌- **Ionic ‌Greek** — Ἰήσων ‌(Iḗsōn), the ​Ionic form ‌with long eta ​standing for ​Attic long alpha
​- **Latin** ‌— Iāsōn, whence ​English 'Jason'

​Iásōn is Tier ​1 because ‌the Greek Ἰάσων ​contains both ​stress (acute ​on the long ‌alpha) and ​length (the long ‌ᾱ and ​the final ω). ‌The restoration ​keeps both: the ‌acute on ‌á and the ​macron on ​ō. The ​name means 'healer' ​— a ‌fact the quest ‌story tends ​to forget.

sources.citation: Liddell-Scott-Jones Greek-English Lexicon, 9th ed. with 1996 supplement, 1940.

domains.body:
Iásōn ​is the ‌captain of ‌the first ​great sea-quest ​of Greek ​myth: the ​voyage of ​the ‌Argo to ​Colchis for ​the Golden ‌Fleece. His ​name comes ‌from **ἰάομαι, ​'to heal'** ‌— ​yet his ​story is ​less about ​curing than ​about gathering: ‌he is ​the hero ‌whose ​greatest power ‌is to ​summon other ‌heroes, and ​to win ‌the love ​of a ​princess ‌whose magic ‌does the ‌work.[^1]

### ​The Argo

​The first ‌true ship, ​built by ​Argos ‌the shipwright ​under Athena's ​direction; its ‌prow held ​a beam ‌from the ​speaking oak ​of ​Dodona.

### ​The Golden ‌Fleece

The ‌fleece of ​the flying ‌ram that ​carried Phrixos ​to ‌Colchis, hung ‌in a ‌grove of ‌Árēs and ​guarded by ‌a sleepless ​dragon.

### ​The ​Argonauts

Some ‌fifty heroes ​— Heraklēs, ​Orpheus, the ​Dioskouroi, Atalanta ‌in some ​tellings — ​the ​greatest muster ‌before Troy.

​### The ‌Healer's Name

​From ἰάομαι, ‌'to heal' ​— the ‌ironic ‌name of ​a hero ​whose cures ​are worked ​by Medea's ‌pharmaka, not ‌his own ​hands.

sources.citation: Etymological Dictionary of Greek, 2 vols., Brill, 2010.

symbols.body:
The ​iconography ‌associated ‌with Iásōn ​concentrates ​in ​a ​small ​set ‌of recurring ​attributes, ​each ‌a ​compressed ‌statement ​about the ‌name:[^1]

​- ​**Golden ​Fleece** ​— ​The object ‌of ​the ‌quest, ​token ‌of the ​kingship ‌to ​be ‌restored
​- ​**The Argo** ‌— ‌The ‌first ​ship; ​its ‌name, 'swift', ​shares ​the ‌shining ​root ​ἀργός
‌- **The ​single ‌sandal** ​— ​The ​sign ​of the ‌oracle ‌— ​the ‌one-sandaled ​man ​who would ‌undo ‌Pelias
‌- ‌**Dragon's ​teeth** ‌— Sown ​in ​Colchis, ​they ‌sprouted ​armed men ​— ​the ‌trial ​Aietēs ​set ​him
- ‌**The ​dove** ‌— ​Loosed ‌at ​the Clashing ‌Rocks ‌on ​Phineus's ​counsel; ​its ​safe passage ‌showed ‌the ​way

sources.citation: Liddell-Scott-Jones Greek-English Lexicon, 9th ed. with 1996 supplement, 1940.

mythology.body:
The myth of ​Iásōn is the myth of ‌the quest itself: an ‌unjust king, an impossible errand, ​a band of heroes, and ​a prize won by ​cunning and love rather than ​by strength alone. Pindar sang ​it; Apollonius made it an ‌epic; Euripides gave it ​its dark ending.[^1]

### The ​Man with One Sandal (The ‌Oracle)

Pelias, who had seized ​the throne of Iolkos ‌from Iásōn's father Aisōn, was ​warned by an oracle to ‌beware the man wearing ​one sandal. Iásōn came down ​from Mount Pelion, where the ​centaur Cheirōn had reared him, ​and lost a sandal ​fording the river Anauros — ‌carrying, Apollodorus says, an old ​woman who was Hera in ‌disguise. Pelias saw the ​sign and set the errand ‌he thought would kill him: ​fetch the Golden Fleece ‌from the edge of the ​world.[^2]

### The Argo and ‌the Clashing Rocks (The Voyage)

​The greatest heroes of ​the age answered the summons. ‌The Argo sailed from Pagasai ‌through wonders and losses — ‌Lemnos, the land of ​women; the death of Hylas, ​which cost them Heraklēs; the ‌boxing of Polydeukēs with ​Amykos — until Phineus, the ​blind seer, told them how ‌to pass the Symplegades, the ​rocks that clashed together. ​A dove was loosed first; ‌when it lost only its ​tail-feathers, the Argonauts rowed through ‌on the rebound, and ​the rocks stood still forever.

​### Medea and the Tasks ​of Aietēs (The Trial)

​In Colchis, King Aietēs set ‌three labors: yoke the fire-breathing ‌bulls, plow the field of ​Árēs, and slay the ‌armed men sprung from a ​dragon's teeth. Hera and Athena ​persuaded Aphrodite to send Eros, ‌and Medea, the king's ‌daughter and a priestess of ‌Hekate, fell in love with ‌the stranger. Her ointment ​made Iásōn proof against fire ‌and iron for a day; ​her counsel felled the dragon's ​brood; her charm sang ​the sleepless guardian to sleep, ‌and the Fleece was taken ​in the night.

### The ​Betrayal at Corinth (The ​Return)

The homecoming was shadowed ‌from the start: in Apollodorus's ​telling Medea had dismembered ​her brother Apsyrtos to slow ​the pursuit, and at Iolkos ‌she tricked Pelias's daughters into ​cutting their father to ‌pieces in a false rite ​of renewal. Exiled to Corinth, ‌Iásōn put Medea aside to ​marry the princess Glaukē. ‌Euripides tells the rest — ‌the poisoned robe, the murdered ​children, the chariot of ​the Sun. Iásōn died as ​he had lived, by the ​Argo: struck in old age ‌by a beam of ‌the rotting ship as he ​slept beneath it.

sources.citation: Etymological Dictionary of Greek, 2 vols., Brill, 2010.
Apollonius Rhodius, Argonautica, Loeb Classical Library, 200 BCE.

syncretism.body:
A ​mortal hero ‌drew ‌no ​foreign cult ​identifications ​of ​the sort ​the ‌Olympians ​attracted; Iásōn's ​syncretism ‌is ​literary and ‌linguistic. ​Rome ‌made him ​Iāsōn ​in epic ​(Valerius ​Flaccus) ​and elegy ‌(Ovid's ​Heroides), ‌and through ​Latin ‌his ​name passed ‌into ​every ‌European language. ​More ​strikingly, ‌Hellenistic Jews ‌adopted ‌Ἰάσων as ​the ​Greek ‌equivalent of ​the ​Hebrew ‌Yehōšūaʿ (Joshua): ​a ​Jason ‌appears among ​the ‌high ​priests of ​Jerusalem ​in ​the books ‌of ‌Maccabees, ​and a ‌Jason ​of Thessalonica ​shelters ‌Paul ‌in the ‌Acts ‌of ​the Apostles. ‌The ​healer's ​name, born ​in ‌Thessaly, ​ended as ​one ​of ‌the bridge-names ​between ​the Greek ​and ‌Hebrew ​worlds.[^1]

Within ‌the ​Greek ‌tradition, closely ​related ‌names ‌in the ​corpus ​include ​[[acheron|Achérōn]], [[achilleus|Achilleús]], ​[[adamas|Adámas]], ‌[[aer|Aḗr]], ‌[[aither|Aithḗr]], and ​[[ananke|Anánkē]].

sources.citation: Liddell-Scott-Jones Greek-English Lexicon, 9th ed. with 1996 supplement, 1940.

cultural-legacy.body: Iásōn ​founded ‌a ‌genre: every ​quest ​narrative, ​from ​the ​medieval ‌grail romances ​to ​the ‌modern ​space ‌voyage, ​retraces the ‌Argo's ​wake. ​The ​very ​word ​'argonaut' became ‌the ​common ‌noun ​for ‌the far-sailing ​adventurer ‌— ​and, ‌by ​derivation, ​'astronaut' and ‌'aquanaut'. ‌William ‌Morris ​retold ​the ‌whole myth ​in ​The ‌Life ​and ​Death ‌of Jason ​(1867); ‌Ray ​Harryhausen's ​film ​Jason ​and the ‌Argonauts ‌(1963) ​fixed ‌the ​image ​for a ‌century ‌of ‌cinema. ‌As ​a ‌given name, ​Jason ​ranked ​among ‌the ​most popular ​in ​the ‌English-speaking ​world ​of ​the late ‌twentieth ​century. ‌The ​restoration ‌Iásōn ​returns to ‌the ‌familiar ​name ​its ​forgotten ​meaning: the ‌healer ‌who ​sailed.[^1]

sources.citation: Liddell-Scott-Jones Greek-English Lexicon, 9th ed. with 1996 supplement, 1940.

archaeology.body: Iolkos, ​the ‌city ‌Iásōn ​was ​born to ​rule, ​lies ​beside ‌modern ​Volos: ​Mycenaean ‌remains ​at ‌Dimini ​and at ‌the ​palace-site ​of ​ancient ​Iolkos ​keep ‌the ​legend ‌anchored, and ​the ‌bay ​of ‌Pagasai, ​the ‌Argo's ​port, ​is ‌the ‌bay of ‌Volos ​itself. ​Across ‌the ​Black ​Sea, ‌Colchis ​is ​historical ‌Georgia, where ​the ‌site ​of ​Vani ​has ​yielded ‌astonishing ‌gold-work ​of ‌the fifth–fourth ​centuries ​BCE; ‌the ‌geographer ‌Strabo ‌reports ​that ‌Colchian ​miners ​washed gold ​from ‌mountain ​streams ​with ​fleeces ‌— ​the ​rationalist's ​explanation for ‌the ​Fleece. ‌No ​temple ‌or ​cult ‌of ‌Iásōn ​is ​securely attested; ​his ​monument ‌was ‌a ​story.[^1]

sources.citation: Liddell-Scott-Jones Greek-English Lexicon, 9th ed. with 1996 supplement, 1940.

homeric-hymns.body: The ​Homeric Hymns ‌are silent ‌about Iásōn, ​and ​the silence ​is generic ​rather ​than evidential: ‌the corpus ​hymns gods, ​not ‌mortal heroes, ​and no ‌hero ​of the ‌quest generation ​— neither ​[[herakles|Hēraklēs]] ​nor Thēseus ​nor [[achilleus|Achilleus]] ​— ‌received a ​hymn of ‌his own. ​The ‌oldest surviving ​witness to ‌the ​myth is ‌instead a ​single passage ​of ‌the Odyssey: ‌the Argo, ‌'known ​to all' ​(πᾶσι μέλουσα), ‌sailing home ​from ​Aietēs past ‌the Planctae, ​which ​would have ‌been dashed ​to pieces ‌'had ​not [[hera|Hera]] ​passed her ​through, ​since Iásōn ‌was dear ‌to her' ​(Od. ‌12.69–72).[^1] Already ​in Homer ​the ‌story needs ‌no telling. ‌What the ‌genre ​of hymn ‌could not ​give ​him, the ​genre of ‌praise did: ​Pindar's ​fourth Pythian ​ode, composed ‌for ​King Arcesilas ​of Cyrene ​in 462 ‌BCE, ​is the ‌oldest substantial ​narrative ‌of the ​voyage and ‌the nearest ‌thing ​to a ​hymn Iásōn ​ever ​received.[^2] Apollonius's ‌epic followed ‌three centuries ​later.[^3]

sources.citation: Homer, Odyssey 12.69–72 (the Argo, 'known to all').
Pindar, Pythian Ode 4.
Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautica.

epithets.body:
- ​**Αἰσονίδης** (Aisonídēs) ‌— 'son ‌of ​Aisōn' — ​the standing ​patronymic ​of the ​Argonautica, where ‌the ​bare name ​Iásōn is ‌often ​withheld for ‌lines at ​a ‌time.[^1]
- ​**μονόκρηπις / ​μονοσάνδαλος** ​(monókrēpis, monosándalos) ​— 'the ​one-sandaled ‌man' — ​the oracle's ‌designation ​of him, ‌in Pindar's ​word ‌and Apollodorus's; ​the lost ‌sandal ​is his ​passport.[^2]
- ‌**ἀρχὸς ‌Ἀργοναυτῶν** — ‌'captain of ​the ​Argonauts' — ‌the functional ​title ​later tradition ‌fixed on ​him; ​the muster ‌at Pagasai ​offered the ‌command ​to Heraklēs, ​who refused ​it ​in his ‌favor.[^1]
- ‌**ὁ ​ἰατήρ** — ‌'the healer' ​— ​not an ‌epithet but ‌the ‌name's own ‌gloss, from ​ἰάομαι; ‌antiquity heard ​his calling ​in ​his name.[^3]

‌The stock ​is ​thin beside ​the gods' ‌formulaic ​titles, and ​honest scholarship ​says ‌so: Iásōn ​is the ‌hero ​of one ‌story, not ​a ‌figure of ‌cult, and ​epic ​gave him ​a role ​rather ‌than a ‌liturgy of ​epithets.

sources.citation: Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautica 1 (the election of the leader).
Pindar, Pythian Ode 4.75; Apollodorus, Library 1.9.7–8 (the one-sandaled man).
Liddell-Scott-Jones, s.v. Ἰάσων and ἰάομαι; Beekes, Etymological Dictionary of Greek.

oracle-sites.body: No ​oracle ever ‌spoke in ‌Iásōn's name; ​his story ​runs on ​other people's ​consultations. The ​founding ‌one is ​Delphi's: Pelias, ​the usurper ‌of Iolkos, ​was warned ‌by the ​god to ‌beware ​the one-sandaled ​man, and ​Pindar preserves ​the oracle's ​terms — ‌the man ​of one ‌sandal, ​whenever he ‌should come ​down from ‌the highlands ​to the ‌plain of ​famous Iolkos.[^1] ​The ‌voyage itself ‌began under ‌an oracular ​sign: at ​Pagasai the ‌Argonauts sacrificed ​to [[apollon|Apóllōn]] ​Embasios, ‌'of Embarkation', ​whose altar ​the company's ‌own seer, ​Idmon, read ‌for omens ​of the ​way.[^2] ​And the ​ship carried ‌its own ‌oracle in ​its timbers: ‌a beam ​cut from ​the ‌speaking oak ‌of Dodona, ‌set in ‌the Argo's ​prow by ‌Athena, which ​spoke to ​the ​crew at ‌the journey's ​turns — ​most memorably ​when it ‌declared, on ​the return, ​that ​the murder ‌of Apsyrtos ​must first ‌be purified ​by Kirke.[^3] ‌Iásōn received ​no shrine ‌and ‌no seat ​of prophecy; ​the Greeks ​put oracles ​in his ‌story, not ‌at his ​tomb.

sources.citation: Pindar, Pythian Ode 4.71–78 (the oracle to Pelias); Apollodorus, Library 1.9.7.
Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautica 1.359–449 (Apollo Embasios; Idmon).
Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautica 1.524–527 and 4.580–591 (the beam of Dodona).

iconography.body: Ancient ​art gave ‌Iásōn one ‌unforgettable image ​and a ​handful ​of stock ​scenes. The ​unforgettable one ‌is on ​an Attic ​red-figure ‌cup painted ​by Douris ‌around 480 ​BCE, now ‌in ​the Vatican: ​the hero ​half-swallowed by ​the Colchian ​dragon, hanging ‌limp ​from its ‌jaws while ​Athena stands ‌by and ​the ‌Fleece hangs ​on its ‌tree — ​the single ​most daring ‌rendering ‌of the ‌fleece-taking, read ​by some ​as the ‌hero ​disgorged, by ​others as ‌his plunge ​into the ​guardian's mouth.[^1] ‌The ​stock scenes ‌are the ​muster and ​departure of ​the ​Argo, the ‌one-sandaled stranger ‌before Pelias, ​the contest ‌with the ​fire-breathing ​bulls, and ‌— above ‌all in ‌later and ‌Roman ​art — ‌the Medea ​cycle: the ​oath before ​the dragon, ‌the ​drugged guardian, ​the flight ​with the ‌Fleece.[^2] His ​attributes ​are few ​and stable: ‌the single ​sandal, the ‌traveler's cloak ​and ‌broad hat ​of a ‌wayfarer, and ‌the Fleece ​itself, ​which the ​painters hang ​on a ‌branch like ‌a second ​sun.[^1]

sources.citation: Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautica 2 and 4 (the fleece-taking); the Douris cup, Museo Gregoriano Etrusco, Vatican.
Ovid, Metamorphoses 7 (the Colchian narrative behind the Roman scenes).

meditation.body:
Iásōn is ​the strangest ‌of the ‌great Greek ​heroes, because ​he is the ​least heroic ​by the ​usual measures. ‌He slays no ​monster unaided; ​the fire-breathing ‌bulls are ​mastered through ‌an ointment, the ​dragon through ‌a lullaby, ​the Fleece ​itself through ​a princess's love. ​His one ​distinctive gift ‌is the ​gift of gathering ‌— the ​summons that ‌brought fifty ​heroes to ‌one beach, and ​the charm ‌that won ​Medea. The ​Greeks half-noticed this: ‌Pindar treats ‌him as ‌the gentle ​answer to ​his homeland's sickness, ‌and the ​tragedians show ​a man ‌perpetually outmatched ​by the powers ​he sets ‌in motion.

​That is ‌why his ending ​is so ​quietly terrible. ​There is ​no grand ‌hubris, no defiance ‌of the ​gods — ‌only drift. ​He owes ​everything to a ‌woman and ‌trades her ‌for a ‌useful marriage, and ​the universe ‌answers in ​kind. The ​man named ​'healer' leaves behind ‌him a ​trail of ​the cut ​and the broken: ‌Apsyrtos, Pelias, ​his own ​children. Perhaps ​that is ‌the lesson the ​myth keeps: ‌a name ​is a ‌task, not ​a possession. Iásōn ‌never healed ‌anyone. The ​name waited, ​and in another ​tongue, on ​another shore, ‌it was ‌carried by ​healers again.[^1]

sources.citation: Liddell-Scott-Jones Greek-English Lexicon, 9th ed. with 1996 supplement, 1940.
